conflict_topics: presence of beef on table-top grills conflicting with Agent D's religious restrictions
whether to retain the leaver's chosen Korean barbecue versus accommodating colleagues' dietary/religious needs
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants state concrete constraints and options (e.g., religious restriction about being at a grill; scheduling constraint).
Agent B initially defends the leaver's choice, creating a brief reopening of the issue before conceding.
Agent A plays a coordinating role: checking facts and proposing alternatives; proposals are concise and practical.
Resolution follows factual clarification (extent of beef cooking) rather than acquiescent politeness.
evaluation.final_reason: After Agent D stated she 'can't be at a table where beef is being cooked' (religious restriction), Agent A said 'this place won't work. We'll have to find somewhere else.' Agent B accepted that ('Yeah, okay. It won't work.'). The group then agreed on a different option (zi char): 'A zi char place is a good idea.' (Agent A) and 'Yeah, zi char works.' (Agent B). Thus the team adjusted by abandoning the Korean barbecue to accommodate Agent D and chose an alternative.
position_change_notes: Agent D maintained a consistent, non-negotiable position: cannot be at a table where beef is being cooked (Turn 12).
Agent A initially accepted cancellation (Round 3), later agreed to check facts when asked (Round 4), and then reaffirmed that the restaurant won't work once it was clarified (Rounds 6–7).
Agent B initially advocated preserving the leaver's chosen restaurant (Turn 8), then accepted the incompatibility after the clarification (Turn 16).
Agent C did not take a conflicting stance; raised a scheduling constraint but did not block the chosen alternative.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 2–3: Agent B asks whether the food is all cooked on the same grill; Agent A says she will check. Questioning but no disagreement.
Turn 4–5: Agent B thanks A for checking; Agent C notes a scheduling constraint (meeting at 2:30). No substantive disagreement over the restaurant.

Turn 6–7: Agent D states 'I don't eat beef.' Agent A responds 'Right. Okay, this place is out then. We'll find somewhere else.' Acknowledged incompatibility and an immediate decision to drop the restaurant in this round.

Turn 8–9: Agent B objects to cancelling because 'She chose that place herself... she was really looking forward to it' and asks to check options; Agent A agrees to delay cancelling and to check. The earlier settlement is reopened.

Turn 10 & 12: Agent B presses to keep the booking; Agent D clarifies 'I can't be at a table where beef is being cooked. It's a religious thing.' This raises the severity of the incompatibility (not just menu options but presence of beef on the grill).

Turn 13–14: Agent A says 'If you can't be at the table, this place won't work. We'll have to find somewhere else.' Agent B again asks to check for other table options. The dispute over whether to keep the booking continues.

Turn 15–16: Agent A clarifies 'the whole restaurant will have beef cooking... it's just not going to work.' Agent B concedes: 'Yeah, okay. It won't work.' The group accepts cancelling the Korean barbecue.
Turn 17–18: Agents propose alternatives (food court, zi char). No substantive disagreement about alternatives at this point.
Turn 19–20: Agent A and Agent B agree that zi char is a good idea. Consensus on alternative.
Turn 21–22: Agent A asks Agent C about timing constraints; Agent C notes some zi char places can be slow. This raises a scheduling consideration but no disagreement.
Turn 23–24: Agent D suggests a specific nearby zi char that is usually quick; Agent A asks Agent C whether that will work. No conflict.
Turn 25–26: Agent C notes a small risk of waiting for dishes; Agent A proposes calling and ordering in advance so food will be ready. Problem addressed; no outstanding disagreement.

substantive_insights: The core incompatibility was not only menu items but the presence of beef being cooked at the table, which for Agent D is a disqualifying religious condition.
Clarifying operational facts about the restaurant (whole-restaurant grilling) was decisive in moving the group to change plans.
The group prioritized inclusivity (accommodating Agent D's religious requirement) while seeking an alternative that still felt special (zi char).
Timing constraints (Agent C's meeting) influenced choice of a faster zi char location and the suggestion to pre-order, showing trade-offs considered.
